textbookText: Functions of pancreas i. Pancreatic juice secreted by exocrine gland contains digestive enzymes such as trypsinogen, amylase, and lipase which digest protein carbohydrates fat respectively. ii. Alpha cells secrete glucagon which converts glycogen into glucose. Beta cells secrete insulin which converts excess glucose to glycogen as reserve food materials. Delta cells secrete somatostatin which regulates secretary activity of alpha and beta cells.
Histology of alimentary canal in frog Figure 8.4.13 T.S. of alimentary canal (schematic)
1. Serosa (visceral peritoneum): It is composed of single layer of squamous epithelium. This layer is replaced by fibrous layer called tunica adventitia in oesophagus.

2. Muscularis: It is made up of muscles - outer longitudinal muscle fibre and inner circular muscle fibres. These muscles are smooth muscles which create peristalsis in alimentary canal. This layer is thicker in stomach.
3. Submucosa: This layer is mainly composed of loose connective tissue which contains elastic fibers, fat, blood vessels, and lymph vessels and nerves

4. Mucosa: This is the innermost layer of alimentary canal which is variously modified and folded and with different types of glands. This layer is mainly concerned with secretion, digestion and absorption of nutrients from the digested food. Mucosa consists of lamina
propria (loose connective tissue), muscularis mucosa (in some parts) and innermost folded layer of columnar epithelial cells.

1. Process of capturing food and ingestion: Frog is a carnivorous; especially insectivorous animal that feeds on insects, earthworms, spiders, snails, fishes and smaller frogs which are captured with the help of sticky and protractible tongue. Mode of catching prey is remarkable. While feeding, the frog sits at a suitable place frequented by insects. When any prey comes close to it, it opens its mouth and suddenly flicks out its sticky tongue and strikes the prey. The prey soon comes in contact with the tongue and gets attached. Now, the tongue is withdrawn into the buccal cavity.

Once the prey is captured and brought into the buccal cavity, it is seized and killed with the help of hook-like and pointed maxilliary and vomerine teeth. Teeth do not chew the food but food is moistened by mucus secreted by goblet cells found in the inner lining of buccal cavity. From the buccal cavity food is pushed back by the beating of cilia on the inner wall of buccal cavity and with the help of inbulging of eyeball. Then, contraction of the pharyngeal wall and by peristalsis in oesophagus, food gets passed through oesophagus, down into the stomach.

Food contains complex organic substances which are not of immediate use as they are insoluble and can’t diffuse or absorbed through the inner lining of the alimentary canal. Such complex foodstuffs are subjected to the physical and chemical changes to transform them into soluble and absorbable form. The physical change or mastication of food is brought about by the peristaltic movements of the alimentary canal, while the chemical changes are brought about by the enzymes or biological catalysts. Enzymes are complex proteins having specific property. In the digestive tract, several glands are present which produce various enzymes and they always act at the optimum body temperature. Proteolytic enzymes digest proteins, amylolytic enzymes digests carbohydrates and lipolytic enzymes digest fats. i. Digestion in buccal cavity and oesophagus: There is neither mechanical nor chemical digestion in the buccal cavity as the buccal cavity is devoid of digestive glands. From the buccal cavity, the prey is directly pushed into oesophagus where it undergoes physical changes to some extent due to constant peristaltic movement of its wall. The inner lining of oesophagus secretes mucus and an inactive pepsinogen enzyme. No digestion occurs in oesophagus. Mucus simply makes the food moist or slippery to pass down easily. ii. Gastric Digestion: Food reaches the stomach and stays there for about 2-3 hours; its wall shows a series of peristaltic movements which brought about the churning of food and mix the food thoroughly with gastric juice secreted by the gastric glands; situated in the inner layer (internal lining) of stomach.
